forces: Clarinet, bass clarinet, two horns, harp and strings
intro: The second movement of Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21, is a theme, seven variations and a coda in 99 bars. René Leibowitz conducts the Paris Chamber Orchestra in a recording on the Dial label that was reviewed in June 1950.

cues.title: Theme, bars 1–11
cues.text: The clarinet plays the theme in bars 1–11. Its phrases divide into two halves of five and a half bars, and bar 6 is the midpoint.
cues.evidence: Mark Gotham, “Analysis Examples – Webern Op. 21 and 24”, Open Music Theory (CC BY-SA), https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/twelve-tone-analysis-examples-webern-op-21-and-24/: Theme, measures 1–11, with phrases divided 5.5 + 5.5 and the midpoint at m. 6; row I8 in the clarinet.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation 1: double canon
cues.text: Variation 1 (bars 11–23) begins as the theme ends. It is a double canon at the quarter note: first violin with cello, second violin with viola.
cues.evidence: Mark Gotham, “Analysis Examples – Webern Op. 21 and 24”, Open Music Theory (CC BY-SA), https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/twelve-tone-analysis-examples-webern-op-21-and-24/: Variation 1, measures 11–23, beginning elided with the theme; a double canon at the quarter note pairing violin 1 with cello and violin 2 with viola.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation 4: the midpoint
cues.text: Variation 4 (bars 45–55) is the midpoint of the movement; Webern described it so himself. Its phrases divide 5 + 1 + 5 bars, with bar 50 at the centre.
cues.evidence: Mark Gotham, “Analysis Examples – Webern Op. 21 and 24”, Open Music Theory (CC BY-SA), https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/twelve-tone-analysis-examples-webern-op-21-and-24/: Variation 4, measures 45–55; “Webern himself describes this variation as the midpoint of the movement”; phrases 5 + 1 + 5 with m. 50 the midpoint.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, New York, 1929
cues.text: Alexander Smallens conducted the League of Composers orchestra in the first performance, at Town Hall, New York, on 18 December 1929. Olin Downes wrote in the New York Times that the audience “laughed it out of court”.
cues.evidence: David H. Miller, “Shadows, wraiths, and amoebas: the distinctive flops of Anton Webern in the United States”, Transposition 10 (2022), https://journals.openedition.org/transposition/6924 : the première under Alexander Smallens on 18 December 1929, and Olin Downes in the New York Times of 19 December 1929: “The audience laughed it out of court”. Wikipedia, “Symphony (Webern)”, gives the Town Hall venue.

cues.title: Coda, bars 89–99
cues.text: The coda (bars 89–99) is related to the theme: its phrases again divide into 5.5 + 5.5 bars, with bar 94 at the centre. Variations 5, 6 and 7 are related to variations 3, 2 and 1.
cues.evidence: Mark Gotham, “Analysis Examples – Webern Op. 21 and 24”, Open Music Theory (CC BY-SA), https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/twelve-tone-analysis-examples-webern-op-21-and-24/: Coda, measures 89–99, related to the theme, midpoint m. 94; Variation 5 related to 3, Variation 6 to 2, Variation 7 to 1.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The item lists the Pro Arte Quartet as well; the review shows that the quartet plays Webern’s Op. 5 and Op. 9 on the same LP, not the Symphony. The review describes the orchestra as members of the Orchestre National.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21, for clarinet, bass clarinet, two horns, harp and strings; the edition and the size of the string section are not stated.
fields.note: The 1950 review describes the ensemble as members of the Orchestre National playing as the Paris Chamber Orchestra, but does not say how many string players took part.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The item date, 1950, is the year of the LP release. The review of June 1950 shows only that the LP had appeared by then.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The ensemble’s name points to Paris; neither source states where the recording was made.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The review gives “Dial 7, $5.95” for the LP containing the Symphony, the Five Movements, Op. 5, and the Six Bagatelles, Op. 9.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The February 1951 issue lists the Symphony as “Dial LP” and refers back to the June 1950 review.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Not stated; the Symphony is on side 1
fields.note: The Internet Archive item places the two movements of the Symphony among the tracks of disc 1, side 1; no matrix or take numbers are given.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Internet Archive LP digitisation project; the item lists the collections vinyl_bostonpubliclibrary and vinyl_estate-of-sam-randlett_records
fields.note: The item metadata names the collections and a scanning-station identifier but no individual transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.value: Not stated; the item was made public on 14 July 2021
fields.note: The public date of the item is an upload date, not the date of the transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digital rip of the LP, with the tracks divided by the digitiser; the ripping note for side 1 reads “scratchy disc”.
fields.note: Movement I, on the same side, was not published because a spectrogram of the file shows that its first minutes are dominated by surface noise. Movement II is the cleaner transfer.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Webern died in 1945, so the work has been in the public domain in the EU and other life-plus-70 countries since 2016. IMSLP lists scans of the 1929 Universal Edition score; its United States status is not established here.
fields.note: Rights in the composition are stated separately from rights in the recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963; the LP was reviewed in June 1950.
fields.note: The United States status of a 1950 recording is not established. The Internet Archive item carries no licence label and belongs to the Archive’s “Unlocked Recordings” collection, whose description says works there may already be in the public domain; its metadata has no restriction flag and the MP3 downloads without a login.

composer.background:
When Peter Stadlen prepared the first performance of Webern’s Piano Variations in Vienna in 1937, the composer covered his score with instructions about expression. One phrase needed more vigour; another was an echo. Webern compared the opening movement to a late Brahms intermezzo. In the preface to his annotated edition, published in 1979, Stadlen recalled a “fervently lyrical mind bent on expressiveness”.

Webern was born in Vienna on 3 December 1883 and grew up in Graz and Klagenfurt, with holidays at Preglhof, the family estate in Carinthia. His mother, Amalie, played the piano and sang; he learnt piano and cello and joined the orchestra of the local concert society. The family played chamber music together. Later, when he was living away from home, he wrote in his letters about the woods and meadows around Preglhof and about his mother’s grave at nearby Schwabegg.
